questions.stem: A student reading Britain's trade statistics finds that in 1760 the country was importing 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton to feed its cotton industry; name the industry this raw cotton was imported for, and give the year by which that import had soared to 22 million pounds.

Gives the year as 1787

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A student is shown the earliest factories in England and told they had come up by a certain decade, while their number multiplied only later; name the decade by which the earliest factories came up, and the century in which their number multiplied.

markingPoints.description: Gives the decade as the 1730s
Gives the century in which the number multiplied as the late eighteenth century

evidence:
The earliest factories in England came up by the 1730s. But it
was only in the late eighteenth century that the number of
factories multiplied.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A student's family in an English village spins yarn that a merchant clothier buys, and he then sends the yarn on to weavers, fullers and dyers, with the finishing done in London before it is exported; explain how this arrangement linked town and countryside, and say how many workers a merchant employed at each stage of production.

markingPoints.description: States that merchants were based in towns while the work was done mostly in the countryside, so a close relationship developed between town and countryside
States that producers worked within their family farms, not in factories, and that merchants controlled the system
States that 20 to 25 workers were employed at each stage of production, so each clothier was controlling hundreds of workers

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Merchants were based in towns but the work was done mostly in the countryside, so a close relationship developed between the two. Producers worked within their family farms, not in factories, and merchants controlled the system. At each stage of production a merchant employed 20 to 25 workers, so each clothier was controlling hundreds of workers.

were produced by a vast number of producers working within
their family farms, not in factories. At each stage of production 20
to 25 workers were employed by each merchant. This meant that
each clothier was controlling hundreds of workers.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A student visits a cotton mill where carding, twisting and spinning, and rolling are all carried out under one roof; explain what the eighteenth-century inventions did for the output of each worker, and say what gathering the processes under one roof made possible.

markingPoints.description: States that the inventions increased the efficacy of each step of production – carding, twisting and spinning, and rolling
States that they enhanced output per worker and made stronger threads and yarn possible
States that one roof and management allowed more careful supervision, a watch over quality and the regulation of labour

answerScheme.modelAnswer: The inventions increased the efficacy of each step of production – carding, twisting and spinning, and rolling – so output per worker rose, enabling each worker to produce more, and stronger threads and yarn became possible. Bringing the processes together under one roof and management allowed more careful supervision, a watch over quality and the regulation of labour.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A student asks why the imposing new mills are so far better known today than the small workshops where cloth was still being made; say what contemporaries found so dazzling about the mills, and what they consequently almost forgot.

markingPoints.description: States that the new mills were imposing and so visible that factories had become an intimate part of the English landscape
States that contemporaries were dazzled by the power of the new technology
States that they concentrated their attention on the mills and almost forgot the bylanes and the workshops where production still continued

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Factories had become an intimate part of the English landscape, and the new mills were so visible and imposing, while the power of the new technology seemed so magical, that contemporaries were dazzled. They concentrated their attention on the mills, almost forgetting the bylanes and the workshops where production still continued.

(c) This allowed more careful supervision over the production process, a watch over quality and the regulation of labour.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A student follows one merchant clothier's wool from purchase to export and wants to show how production worked before factories came up; show in steps (a) the route the wool and the spun yarn took, (b) how merchants and the countryside fitted together in this system, and (c) how many workers a merchant employed at each stage of production and what that made him.

markingPoints.description: Traces the route: wool bought from a wool stapler, carried to the spinners, then the spun yarn to weavers, fullers and then dyers
States that the finishing was done in London before the export merchant sold the cloth in the international market
States that merchants were based in towns while the work was done mostly in the countryside, so a close relationship developed between the two

States that 20 to 25 workers were employed at each stage of production, so each clothier was controlling hundreds of workers

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A student is comparing Britain's industrial growth across two phases and then follows the demand for iron and steel; show in steps (a) which industry led the first phase of industrialisation and up to when, (b) which industry led the way after that and when and where railways began to expand, and (c) the value of the iron and steel Britain was exporting by 1873.

markingPoints.description: Names cotton as the leading sector in the first phase of industrialisation
Gives the end of that first phase as the 1840s
States that after that the iron and steel industry led the way
States that railways expanded in England from the 1840s and in the colonies from the 1860s, so demand for iron and steel increased rapidly
States that by 1873 Britain was exporting iron and steel worth about £ 77 million

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) Cotton, growing at a rapid pace, was the leading sector in the first phase of industrialisation up to the 1840s.
(b) After that the iron and steel industry led the way; with the expansion of railways, in England from the 1840s and in the colonies from the 1860s, the demand for iron and steel increased rapidly.
(c) By 1873 Britain was exporting iron and steel worth about £ 77 million.

evidence:
metals. Growing at a rapid pace, cotton was the leading sector in the
first phase of industrialisation up to the 1840s. After that the iron
and steel industry led the way. With the expansion of railways, in

England from the 1840s and in the colonies from the 1860s, the
demand for iron and steel increased rapidly.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A student is examining why Indian businessmen who supplied the capital for many industries had so little say in how those industries were run; show in steps (a) which three European Managing Agencies were the biggest, (b) how these Agencies operated, and (c) who provided the capital, who took the decisions, and what Indian businessmen were not allowed to join.

markingPoints.description: States that European Managing Agencies controlled a large sector of Indian industries
Names the three biggest as Bird Heiglers & Co., Andrew Yule, and Jardine Skinner
States that the Agencies mobilised capital, set up joint-stock companies and managed them
States that in most instances Indian financiers provided the capital while the European Agencies made all investment and business decisions
States that the European merchant-industrialists had their own chambers of commerce which Indian businessmen were not allowed to join

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) Three of the biggest were Bird Heiglers & Co., Andrew Yule, and Jardine Skinner.
(b) The Agencies mobilised capital, set up joint-stock companies and managed them.
(c) In most instances Indian financiers provided the capital while the European Agencies made all investment and business decisions, and the European merchant-industrialists had their own chambers of commerce which Indian businessmen were not allowed to join.

questions.stem:
Till this time, cloth production was spread all over the countryside and carried out within village households. Then Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill. The costly new machines could be purchased, set up and maintained in the mill, and within the mill all the processes were brought together under one roof and management. This allowed a more careful supervision over the production process, a watch over quality, and the regulation of labour, all of which had been difficult to do when production was in the countryside. So visible were the imposing new mills, so magical seemed to be the power of new technology, that contemporaries were dazzled.

Read the case and answer the three questions below, each in one line. (i) Name the person who created the cotton mill. questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
The most dynamic industries in Britain were clearly cotton and metals. Growing at a rapid pace, cotton was the leading sector in the first phase of industrialisation up to the 1840s. After that the iron and steel industry led the way. With the expansion of railways, in England from the 1840s and in the colonies from the 1860s, the demand for iron and steel increased rapidly. By 1873 Britain was exporting iron and steel worth about £ 77 million.

Read the case and answer the three questions below, each in one line. (i) Name the two industries that were the most dynamic in Britain. (ii) State which industry led the first phase of industrialisation, up to when, and which industry led the way after that. (iii) A student claims Britain's industrialisation depended only on cotton; use the case to explain why that is not a fair reading.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Cotton and metals. (ii) Cotton led the first phase up to the 1840s; after that iron and steel led the way. (iii) Iron and steel became the leading sector after the 1840s, and expanding railways from the 1840s in England and the 1860s in the colonies sent demand for it soaring, so cotton was not the whole of industrialisation.

demand for iron and steel increased rapidly.
